item.title: Optical Waveguides Replace Liquid Cooling Loops in New Climate Modeling Clusters
item.description:
ZURICH — Meteorological research centers upgrading supercomputers for kilometer-scale storm forecasting are bypassing copper backplanes in favor of silicon-photonic waveguides that move data with infrared pulses rather than electrical currents.

High-resolution atmospheric models exchange petabytes of boundary values between adjacent server racks every second. Moving those bits electrically turns nearly half of a facility’s power draw into waste heat, forcing operators to install massive evaporative cooling towers.

Lowering Water Demand Alongside Kilowatts

By replacing short-reach copper cables with co-packaged optical engines, pilot installations cut cluster cooling water consumption by 38 percent during summer peaks without slowing convection-resolving simulations.

item.title: Co-Packaged Optical Interconnects Target Copper Bottlenecks Inside Data Centers
item.description:
EINDHOVEN — Network switch engineers are moving optical transceivers off pluggable front-panel cages and mounting silicon photonics engines millimeter-close to switch silicon to break power and heat limits inside dense compute clusters.

At modern signaling speeds, pushing electrical bits even thirty centimeters across printed circuit copper traces burns a growing share of rack electricity and forces aggressive liquid cooling loops.

Shorter Copper Paths, Lower Heat

By converting data into modulated laser light right beside the switching die, co-packaged optics halve interconnect energy per bit while leaving existing building fiber trunks intact.
